question: You double the number of Monte Carlo samples. What happens to the width of the confidence interval?
options: It stays the same once N is above 30
It shrinks by a factor of 4, as variance falls with N^2
It halves, because the error is proportional to 1/N
It shrinks by about 1.41x (sqrt 2)
explanation: Width scales as 1/sqrt(N): doubling N divides it by sqrt 2. Halving it needs 4x the samples.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: Your service-time data are strongly right-skewed. After averaging 400 replications, what is approximately normal?
options: Neither: skewed data never give normal means
The service times, because n is now large
Both the data and the mean, by the CLT
The distribution of the replication mean
explanation: The CLT applies to the mean, not to the raw data, which keep their shape.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: Customers arrive independently at a constant average rate. What does that imply about the times between arrivals?
options: Uniform between zero and twice the mean gap
Exponential: short gaps are the most common
Normally distributed around the mean gap
Roughly equal gaps, all close to the mean gap
explanation: The Poisson process axioms imply exponential gaps (Theorem 23.3), whose density is highest at zero: arrivals cluster.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A single-server queue runs at 80% utilisation. Demand grows so that it runs at 90%. Roughly what happens to the mean wait in M/M/1?
options: It grows about 12.5%, in line with demand
It grows by about 10 percentage points
It roughly doubles
It stays similar: there is spare capacity
explanation: W = 1/(mu - lam): at mu = 1, lam 0.8 -> 5 and 0.9 -> 10. Queues are nonlinear near rho = 1.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A time-stepped model gives slightly different answers when you halve the step. What is the safest conclusion?
options: Halving a step always makes answers worse
Truncation error is not yet negligible
The model is wrong and has to be rebuilt
The random seed changed between the two runs
explanation: Changing results under step refinement indicate discretisation error; a convergence study (L100 #4, Theorem 24.1) tells you when it is small enough.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: An explicit solver on a model with a fast-decaying component blows up unless the step is tiny, although the solution is smooth. What is the cause?
options: Round-off error, because the steps are tiny
A hidden discontinuity the solver cannot see
Stiffness: stability, not accuracy, limits h
A bug: smooth solutions cannot go unstable
explanation: Explicit methods must keep h lam inside their stability region even when the solution is smooth (Theorem 24.3).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: You make a finite-difference step h smaller and smaller. What happens to the error?
options: It keeps falling towards zero as h shrinks
It rises steadily: small steps are worse
It stays constant once h is below 1e-3
It falls, then rises again due to round-off
explanation: Truncation falls with h but round-off grows like u/h; the best h is near sqrt(eps) for a forward difference (Theorem 24.4).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: Eight parallel workers each run replications with the same fixed seed. What will the pooled results look like?
options: Copies of one run; a falsely narrow CI
Eight independent samples, one per worker
A crash: generators cannot share one seed
Slightly correlated but mostly valid samples
explanation: Same seed means same stream: the 'replications' are copies (L300 #16's fault). Use SeedSequence.spawn.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A random number generator passes a chi-square uniformity test. What does that show?
options: That its period is long enough for any run
That it is suitable for every simulation
Only that this test did not reject it
That its outputs are truly and fully random
explanation: Tests can only reject; RANDU passes 1-D tests and fails in 3-D (Theorem 25.2).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: When does pairing each U with 1 - U (antithetic variates) reduce variance?
options: Only when the number of samples is even
When f(U), f(1 - U) are anti-correlated
Always, as each pair balances itself out
Only when f is symmetric about u = 0.5
explanation: The gain is 1/(1 + rho); for symmetric f, rho = +1 and the variance doubles (Theorem 25.4).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: What is the difference between verification and validation of a simulation?
options: They are two synonyms for testing a model
Verification: built right? Validation: right model?
Users verify; developers validate the model
Verification uses data; validation uses unit tests
explanation: Verification checks the implementation against the conceptual model; validation checks accuracy for the intended purpose (Sargent).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A model is tuned on 2025 data and then reported as 'validated' because it fits 2025 data well. What is wrong?
options: Validation needs controlled experiments only
It should be tuned on older 2024 data instead
Tuning-data fit is not validity evidence
Nothing: a good fit is what validity means
explanation: Validate on data not used for fitting (time-ordered holdout), as L300 #13 shows with the poly-6 failure.
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A model reproduces last year's grade distribution exactly. What does that tell you about individual students?
options: Little: many can still be misgraded
Every student got the grade they would earn
Errors cancel, so individuals do not matter
Each individual error is at most one grade
explanation: Aggregate fit is compatible with large individual disagreement (lesson 26: distribution error 0.0000, exact agreement 40.0%).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: Two staffing policies are compared by simulation. Which approach gives the sharpest comparison for the same number of runs?
options: Common random numbers for both policies
Independent seeds per policy to avoid bias
Average both policies' outputs, then compare
One long run per policy, ignoring warm-up
explanation: CRN induces positive correlation, so Var(difference) shrinks (L200 #11: +/-0.44 -> +/-0.12).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)

question: A queue simulation starts empty and you average waits from time 0. What bias do you expect?
options: Initialisation bias: early waits are too short
Bias only if the random seed is chosen badly
Waits that are too long: the server starts cold
None: the long-run average removes it at once
explanation: An empty start understates congestion in a queue that is usually busy; delete a warm-up period and use enough replications (L200 #10).
use: pre-test (week 1) and post-test (week 14); report normalised gain g = (post - pre)/(100 - pre)
